scenario: AITA for asking my boyfriend to pick up and drop off my child on weekends which made him suggest a break up? | So for full disclosure my partner works full time and is usually at work from 7am-7pm, and I have a weekend job that requires me to be away from 9am-12pm. We don’t live together but we are local so we are always in and out of each other’s homes. My son decided he wanted to play football on weekends- he’s 12 years old and really excited about it. I was initially going to ask my bf if he could pay for it but I mentioned it to my mum when I went around for a cup of tea and she was strongly expecting me to pay and told me it was my responsibility not my bf’s... even though he’s been in my life 3 years. So I ended up having to pay but in order to afford it I extended my hours at work to 9-5. I asked my bf if he’d be willing to pick up and drop off my son on weekends as obviously if be at work and he looked uncomfortable and said sorry no can’t his dad drop him? I admit I snapped at him and told him that his dad lives in south London whereas we live in north London and his dad doesn’t drive but my boyfriend does. I asked him if he really wanted to be part of this family and if he did he wouldn’t mind doing small stuff like this for me. I suppose his dad COULD take him but what would be a 1 hour + journey for his dad would take 15 minutes for my bf. He got really angry and told me that he was having to work longer hours to support me and my son and that he wanted to use his weekends to go to football games etc as I wasn’t at home anyway. He said that he wanted to chill and relax and that I was forcing things on him way too quick. He then suggested that we break up bc ”I was putting too many responsibilities on him” and I was like.. really? Over a bloody football game? Welcome to the real world love! The little sneak then went over to see my mum and had a heart to heart with her which ended up in HER calling ME and her telling me I am out of line. Who is TA? AITA?

prediction.raw: **1** (Yes, you are the asshole) **Why:** - **You're the parent, not him.** As the biological parent, *you* are responsible for your child's logistics (transportation, schedules, etc.). His role is *not* to be a substitute parent or de facto chauffeur, especially since you don't live together and he has no legal or societal obligation to承担 these duties. - **"Part of the family" is not a free pass.** Just because he's been in your life 3 years doesn't mean he's automatically responsible for your child's needs. "Being part of the family" is about emotional support, not *practical* parenting tasks. Framing it as "if you really wanted to be part of this family, you wouldn't mind" is emotionally manipulative and unfair. - **You ignored his boundaries.** He works 7am–7pm mon– Fri (12-hour shifts), so weekends are his only time to rest. A 15-minute drop-off * sounds* small, but for someone exhausted from long workdays, it’s still a * request* that requires his time and energy. He有权 prioritize his own well-being, especially when you haven't discussed shared responsibilities or mutual expectations. - **You passed the buck to him.** You extended your work hours to afford football costs, but then * didn't* arrange transportation yourself. Instead, you assumed he * must* step in because "his dad lives far away and doesn't drive." But his dad is * still* an option ( even if it's a longer drive for him), and * you* should be the one to coordinate it—not him. - **Your " real world" comment was dismissive.** Telling him " Welcome to the real world" implies he's being unreasonable for wanting boundaries, but * you* are the one who's overstepping. Real-world parenting means * you* handle the logistics, not that your partner must sacrifice their time to " support" you. - **Your own mum agrees.** She explicitly told you " it's your responsibility, not his" and later called you " out of line"—which aligns with societal norms. If even your closest ally thinks you're wrong, that's a clear sign. **What you should do:** - **Take ownership of your child's needs.** Arrange transportation yourself ( carpool with other parents, school programs, or adjust your work schedule). - **Respect his boundaries.** If he's not ready to be deeply involved in your child's life, that's his choice. Pushing him to " prove" his commitment through practical tasks is unfair. - **Communicate * before* making demands.** If you want him to help with logistics, discuss it openly * as a couple* ( e.g., " I'm struggling with drop-offs—could we talk about how we might share this?"). But never guilt-trip him into it. **Bottom line:** This isn't about " a bloody football game"— it's about you expecting him to * be* a parent when he's not. That's not fair to him, and it's not how healthy relationships work. **TA.**

- Boyfriend's dad lives in South London, doesn't drive, so picking up would be 1+ hour for him vs 15 mins for boyfriend. 
- User asked boyfriend to do drop-off/pick-up "as a small thing" for "being part of the family," but he refused, citing work fatigue and wanting weekend relaxation. 
- Mum sided with boyfriend, saying user was "out of line."

- He's not legally obligated to help with the child's logistics. 
- User's mum said " it's your responsibility, not his" - which aligns with standard societal norms. 
- But user feels he *should* help because he's " in the family" - but " family" isn't defined by cohabitation or time together. 

**2. The ask itself:** 
- Pick up/drop off for a 12yo's football practice is a * reasonable* request... * if* it's within his capacity. 
- But: 
  - He works 7-7 mon-fri (12-hour shifts), so weekends are his only downtime. 
  - User extended her work hours to 9-5 to afford football costs - so she's * also* working weekends now. 
  - If she's at work 9-5, * she* can't drop off either. 
  - So who * is* supposed to do it? 
  - Boyfriend's dad is an option but it's a 1+ hour journey for him vs 15 mins for boyfriend. 
  - But... is it * fair* to expect the boyfriend to do it when he's not the parent? 

**3. "Forcing responsibilities too quick":** 
- Boyfriend says he's " working longer hours to support me and my son" - but user didn't mention him * financially* supporting them. 
- User paid for football herself ( after mum's " it's your responsibility" comment). 
- So " support" might mean emotional support? But he's not * working* extra hours for them - he's working his own 7-7 job. 
- His " support" claim feels... off. Unless he's literally paying for things? User didn't specify. 

**4. The " small stuff" framing:** 
- User called it " small stuff," but for someone working 12-hour shifts mon-fri, a 15-minute drop off might * feel* like a big ask if it's on top of his own needs. 
- But... 15 minutes is * literally* 15 minutes. 
- However, if he's * also* working weekends ( user didn't say he does, but she extended her hours to 9-5, so she's at work 9-5 on weekends - but what about him? )

- But the * only* options are: 
  - Boyfriend's dad ( 1+ hour drive for him) 
  - Boyfriend ( 15 mins)

- User's " Welcome to the real world" is... not helpful. 
- It's not about " real world" vs " not real world" - it's about * boundaries* and * mutual respect*. 
- A 12yo's football practice is a * normal* responsibility for a parent, but the boyfriend is * not* the parent.

**6. Mum's involvement:**

- Then she called user " out of line" - which aligns with her earlier stance. 
- So even the user's own mum agrees the ask was inappropriate. 

**7. Breakup suggestion:** 
- Boyfriend suggested break up over " too many responsibilities" - but the * only* " responsibility" he's being asked to take on is a 15-minute drop off. 
- But... if he's * already* feeling overburdened ( " working longer hours to support me" - though user didn't clarify this), then maybe he's not ready for this level of involvement. 
- The " real" issue might be that he's not ready to be " part of the family" in a practical way, and user misinterpreted " being in the family" as * de facto* co-parenting. 

**8. AITA verdict:** 
- User asked for a * specific* favor ( drop off) that * could* be reasonable... but: 
  - She frames it as " if you're part of the family, you wouldn't mind" - which is emotional manipulation. 
  - She didn't consider his work schedule or need for downtime. 
  - She's the parent - * she* should arrange transportation. 
  - Boyfriend's dad is an option, even if it's longer for him. 
  - " small stuff" is subjective - for a person working 12-hour shifts mon-fri, a 15-minute drop off might * feel* like a big ask if it's on top of his own needs. 
  - But... 15 minutes is * literally* 15 minutes. 
  - However, the * bigger* issue is the * expectation* that he * must* do this because he's " in the family" - which is not how relationships work. 
  - He's not obligated to be a substitute parent. 
  - User's " real world" comment shows she's not taking responsibility for her own child's logistics. 
  - Mum's " out of line" confirms this. 

**Final judgment:** 
- **User is the asshole (TA)**. 
- Why:

  - She's asking her * non-parent* boyfriend to do it " because he's part of the family" - but " part of the family" doesn't mean " de facto parent." 
  - She didn't consider his work schedule or need for weekend rest. 
  - She's using guilt (" if you really wanted to be part of this family...") which is manipulative. 
  - Her " real world" comment shows she's not taking ownership of her own parenting duties. 
  - Even her own mum agrees she's " out of line." 
  - The boyfriend's " working longer hours to support me" claim is... questionable ( user didn't specify financial support), but the * core issue* is that he's not obligated to be the child's transportation.
